source_read: PMC HTML, PMC9310449 (full text read in own browser tab: abstract, introduction, methods, results incl. Tables 1-2, qualitative themes, discussion, limitations, declarations). Figure 1 (practice prevalence and Harm Reduction Scores) not read as an image; the claims' statements about it rest on the running text. Online supplement (Tables S1-S3) not read.

claims.overstatement: None found; the claim is more cautious than the authors, whose discussion calls the correlations preliminary evidence that the practices may reduce negative and enhance positive experiences.
claims.note: Every Palmer number in statement and magnitude checked. Editors' intervals recomputed (Fisher z, n = 163): r = -0.21 -> -0.352 to -0.058; r = -0.15 -> -0.297 to +0.004; r = 0.24 -> 0.090 to 0.380; r squared 2.2%, 4.4%, 5.8% (claim's 2 to 6%): all match. Two details the claim could add if space allows: the CEQ was given with two of its three Insanity items missing (experimenter error), and one listed practice (arranging a time to take the dose) had no importance scores, so it added nothing to anyone's score. The importance ratings could be negative (-10 to +10), so practices the sample judged unhelpful subtracted from the score.

anchors.locator: Methods > Design (1st paragraph); Methods > Participants (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Observational repeated-measures online survey, pre-registered on OSF (osf.io/35kbs). Opportunistic recruitment through university societies and online psychedelic communities. Eligibility: 18 or over, a classic psychedelic or analogue used at least twice in life, fluent English; neither the first nor the most recent experience in a research or therapy setting, and neither a microdose (self-defined). The two-use minimum excludes anyone who stopped after one use.

anchors.locator: Results > Participant characteristics and psychedelic use history (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: n = 163 after exclusions (many excluded for failed attention checks). Age mean 27.5 (SD 8.06), median 26, range 18-56; 120 male, 35 female, 8 non-binary (73.6% male). Lifetime psychedelic uses mean 28.4 (SD 45.2), mode 20, median 11.5.

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows 'How long ago in months' (mean, mode, median)
anchors.extracted: First experience: mean 67.52 months (SD 78.33), mode 24, median 42. Most recent: mean 8.68 (SD 20.76), mode 1, median 2.

anchors.locator: Methods > Measures > Harm reduction practices (1st and 2nd paragraphs); Methods > Procedure (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Practice list compiled from online harm reduction resources, literature and colleagues, split into before, during (including some 'myths') and after. Participants ticked the practices used for each experience and, at the end of the same online sitting (after recalling both experiences and completing CEQ and EBI for each), rated each practice's importance for a safe experience from -10 (detrimental) to +10 (extremely helpful). Practice score = sample mean rating; Participant Harm Reduction Score = sum of the practice scores of the practices a person used (after-practices included). 'Arranged a time to take the dose' had no scores (methodological error).

anchors.locator: Results > Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences (2nd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Participant Harm Reduction Score with EBI: r = 0.24, p = 0.002, for both experiences; with first-experience CEQ: r = -0.21, p = 0.006; with most-recent CEQ: r = -0.15, p = 0.061 (no statistical evidence). Unadjusted bivariate correlations. Editors' 95% intervals (Fisher z, n = 163): 0.09 to 0.38; -0.35 to -0.06; -0.30 to 0.00.

anchors.locator: Results > Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences (2nd paragraph); Table 2, row 'Harm Reduction Score'
anchors.extracted: Repeated-measures ANOVA, time (before, during, during-myths, after) x occasion: main effect of occasion F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001; occasion x time interaction. Bonferroni comparisons, most recent vs first: before t = -9.63, p < 0.001; after t = -3.28, p = 0.03; during t = -1.47, p = 1; during-myths t = -0.04, p = 1. Score mean (SD): first 40.06 (18.90), most recent 48.68 (18.81).

anchors.locator: Methods > Measures > Challenging Experience Questionnaire (1st paragraph); Results > Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences (1st paragraph); Table 2, rows 'CEQ' and 'EBI'
anchors.extracted: CEQ: 26 items, seven subscales, 0-5 ratings, scored as % of maximum; two of the three Insanity items were not asked (experimenter error). CEQ mean (SD): first 17.14 (18.06), most recent 17.29 (17.06); subscale x occasion ANOVA showed no meaningful differences. EBI higher for most recent (39.18 vs 27.77; t(162) = 4.42, p < 0.001, d = 0.35). CEQ and EBI positively correlated (r = 0.393 first, 0.369 most recent).

anchors.locator: Results > Qualitative analysis > Theme 2 Importance of the drug (2nd paragraph); Subtheme 3.3 Tripping alone versus in company (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Testing the drug and getting it from a reputable source both had high practice scores; few participants tested their drugs, many obtained them from a reputable source, especially for the most recent experience. The majority were with trusted friends on both occasions (high practice score); few had an unintoxicated trip sitter present (low practice score). Values are shown only in Figure 1.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Strengths, limitations and future directions (2nd and 3rd paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Authors: sample from forums and organisations with a special interest in psychedelics, largely male; possible survivor bias, since people who stayed engaged and kept using may have had fewer unpleasant first experiences; recall of the first experience may be subject to forgetting, and post-trip meaning-making may have changed memories.

Authors read the correlations as preliminary evidence that the practices may reduce negative and enhance positive experiences, and as lending credibility to the participants' importance ratings (a circular check, since the ratings weight the score).

claims.overstatement: None; the claim states that the comparison was untested.
claims.note: Palmer part only. 19.27 vs 16.77 and 31.46 vs 16.16 (rounded to 19/17 and 31/16) and n = 24 and 12 match Table 2 and the text. Home or a friend's house: 72% of first and 75% of most recent experiences. Two qualifications: (1) Table 1 lists 6 festival and 8 club experiences for the most recent occasion (14), not the 12 party-setting experiences in Table 2 and the text, an unexplained discrepancy; (2) the first-experience difference is small against SDs of about 18 (about 0.14 SD), and the most-recent difference rests on 12 people whose harm reduction scores were also much lower.

anchors.extracted: First experience: home 67 (41%), trusted friend's house 51 (31%), nature 18 (11%), festival 11 (7%), club 8 (5%), ceremonial 0, house party 3, outdoor party 2, unclear 2, school 1. Most recent: home 93 (57%), friend's house 29 (18%), nature 19 (12%), festival 6 (4%), club 8 (5%), ceremonial 4 (2%), unclear 4. Festival + club for the most recent experience = 14, against 12 party-setting experiences in Table 2.

anchors.locator: Results > Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences (3rd paragraph); Table 2, columns 'Party setting' and 'Other setting'
anchors.extracted: Unplanned exploratory comparison of party/club/festival vs other settings, no statistical tests (large difference in group sizes). n = 24 vs 139 (first), 12 vs 151 (most recent). CEQ % of maximum, mean (SD): first 19.27 (18.02) vs 16.77 (18.10); most recent 31.46 (24.02) vs 16.16 (15.96). Harm Reduction Score lower in party settings (21.95 vs 43.20; 26.23 vs 50.46). EBI lower in party settings for the first experience (20.38 vs 29.05) but not the most recent (41.56 vs 39.00).

anchors.locator: Discussion > Strengths, limitations and future directions (5th paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Authors call these analyses exploratory and underpowered; their sentence that party use went with lower EBI holds only for the first experience (Table 2).

key_findings.note: House party 3 (2%) + outdoor party 2 (1%) = 5 of 163, 3%, as the card combines them.
d = 0.35 equals t / sqrt(n) = 0.346, as the card's analysis field says.
Intervals recomputed independently before opening the card: identical.
All seven most-recent subscales are numerically higher in party settings, as stated.
Discussion paragraph numbering checked: 3rd (purpose, dose, timing), 4th (comfortable surroundings, highest score), 5th (trusted friends, sober sitter), 6th (rest day, talking afterwards).

The source says the last two practices are recommended only for more experienced users; that they come from harm-reduction websites follows from Methods (list built from online harm reduction resources) and Subtheme 3.2.
The count of 61 coded comments is printed in Methods > Statistical analysis (1st paragraph), a place the locator could add.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: F(1,162) = 28.32 gives partial eta squared 0.149; F(3,486) = 563.82 gives 0.777.
Found independently in step 1. Weighted means recomputed: with 12/151 the subgroup means give 48.68 (HR) and 17.29 (CEQ), the printed overall values; with 14/149 they would give 48.38 and 17.47.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall follows from no adjustment at all (confounding), recalled self-weighted exposure that includes after-use practices, and survivor selection; the domain judgments match what I found.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial on the none/minor/substantial/severe scale: hedged wording, but a causal reading of r of about 0.2, a circular 'credibility' argument for the ratings, an abstract that blurs the null most-recent CEQ result, and a limitations sentence that misstates EBI by setting.
